source.abstract: ABSTRACT Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) dominate visual computing, but their electronic implementations face fundamental bottlenecks in speed and energy efficiency. Although photonic alternatives offer a promising route, all‐optical image recognition using CNNs remains challenging in experiments due to the difficulty of implementing effective weak‐light nonlinearities. Here, we demonstrate a streamlined all‐optical CNN architecture with only physically guided, fixed convolutional and trainable fully‐connected layers (FCLs), which circumvents explicit, energy‐intensive nonlinear layers. Our design leverages a fixed multi‐kernel metasurface operator to perform 24 directional‐differentiation convolutions, thus enhancing feature orthogonality and suppressing crosstalk. This preprocessing enables the system to exploit the weak nonlinearity produced by square‐law detection, thereby achieving high experimental classification accuracy: 86.8% on MNIST and 94.8% on ten‐class gesture recognition. The system exhibits high reconfigurability and robustness. Its all‐optical inference core achieves an equivalent computational throughput of 1.13 × 10 5 TOPS and an energy efficiency of 1.88 × 10 3 TOPS/W—surpassing current CNN implementations. At the system level, it achieves an end‐to‐end throughput of 871 TOPS and an energy efficiency of 4.97 TOPS/W, still exceeding advanced all‐electronic devices and paving the way for ultralow‐latency intelligent hardware.

source.abstract: Optical convolutional neural networks (OCNNs) are susceptible to modulation, alignment, and detection errors, which cause the accuracy of a deployed optical–electronic network to deviate from its numerical model. We propose a learnable bit-plane weighted-fusion (AWF) strategy for low-dimensional offline calibration after camera detection. Each 8-bit input image is decomposed into eight binary planes, convolved separately, and reconstructed using eight learnable normalized weights before electronic activation, pooling, and classification. With 5000 MNIST training images, the optical neural network (ONN) using AWF reaches 92.6% training accuracy, 1.9% points above the traditional binary weighted-fusion (TWF) method. The corresponding experimentally measured test accuracies are 90.30% and 88.69%, respectively. Under 5 dB added noise, AWF-ONN maintains 83.84% accuracy, 5.51% points above TWF, while its loss relative to the no-added-noise condition is 6.46% points compared with 10.36% points for TWF-ONN. A two-layer network retains an experimental advantage of 1.12% points. The results show that a low-dimensional calibration of bit-plane contributions can improve optical inference when labeled data or signal-to-noise ratio is limited.
